name: bstr (byte strings with reusable Finder and line iteration)
baseline: std line-by-line search: BufRead::read_line into a String, then str::contains
verdict_reason: The author's grep-style program ran 2.80x faster than the std version, but only 1.29x of that came from skipping UTF-8 validation; the rest came from building the searcher once and avoiding a copy. The test was run in September 2022, before Rust 1.67 added the SSE2 short-needle path to str::contains, which removes much of the per-call setup the post blamed for about 25% of the std program's runtime. The gap today is likely smaller; no newer measurement was found.
tier_reason: First-party blog post with full program listings and hyperfine output, but no CPU, OS or rustc version.
claimed_speedup: 2.80x faster end to end (252.9 ms vs 707.7 ms) with Finder plus for_byte_line_with_terminator; 2.15x (329.6 ms vs 708.1 ms) with Finder alone; 1.29x (549.6 ms vs 710.2 ms) for the same contains call on bytes instead of a String
workload: Print every line containing 'Sushi' from a Rust source file duplicated five times (/tmp/rust.5x.rs) read on stdin; hyperfine with 5 warmup runs.
platforms: All Rust targets; no_std with or without alloc
one_liner: Byte-string extension traits for &[u8]; a line-by-line grep ran 2.8x faster than String plus str::contains, measured before Rust 1.67.
how_it_is_fast: bstr works on &[u8], so lines need no UTF-8 validation. Its Finder (memchr::memmem underneath) is built once and reused for every line instead of being rebuilt per contains call, and BufReadExt::for_byte_line_with_terminator hands out lines straight from the reader's buffer without copying them into a caller-owned buffer.
use_it_when: Line-oriented processing of files that may not be valid UTF-8, such as logs or source trees
The same needle searched across many lines or records
skip_it_when: Data is already a &str and is searched once
Downstream code needs guaranteed-valid UTF-8 strings
caveats: Measured before Rust 1.67's str::contains SSE2 path for short needles; 'Sushi' is a 5-byte needle that path covers
No hardware or rustc version stated
One workload with a rare match; dense matches would shift time to output
tradeoffs: Byte strings carry no UTF-8 guarantee; APIs that need &str still require validation

evidence.quote: a significant portion of the runtime of our program (~25% from a quick glance at a profile) is the construction of the substring searcher
